title: Type erasure — compiler erases generics, consequences: no new T(), no instanceof List<String>, bridge methods
shortTitle: Type erasure — compiler erases generics, consequences: no new T(), no instanceof List<String>, bridge methods

s1_definition.profdef: **Type erasure** means the Java compiler enforces generic type safety at COMPILE time, then ERASES all type parameters before generating bytecode. `List<String>` becomes just `List` at runtime. `T` becomes `Object` (or the bound, e.g., `T extends Number` → `Number`). **Consequences**: (1) `new T()` illegal — compiler doesn't know what T is at runtime. (2) `instanceof List<String>` illegal — at runtime, it's just `List`. (3) Generic exception types illegal — `catch (T e)` impossible. (4) **Bridge methods** generated for covariant overrides — if a subclass narrows a return type, the compiler generates a bridge method with the erased signature that delegates to the specific one.
s1_definition.analogy: Generics are like LABELS on filing drawers during work hours (compile time): "This drawer is for Cheques ONLY." The label prevents you from putting a withdrawal form in the cheque drawer. But at the END OF THE DAY (runtime), all labels are RIPPED OFF (erasure). Every drawer just says "Object." This means: at runtime, you can't ask "Is this a cheque drawer?" (instanceof List<String>) — all drawers look the same. You can't say "Create a new whatever-is-in-this-drawer" (new T()) — the label is gone.
s1_definition.oneliner: Generics = compile-time labels. Type erasure = labels removed at runtime. At runtime: List<String> = List<Integer> = List. No new T(), no instanceof, bridge methods for covariant overrides.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** **Type erasure** means the Java compiler enforces generic type safety at COMPILE time, then ERASES all type parameters before generating bytecode. `List<String>` becomes just `List` at runtime. `T` becomes `Object` (or the bound, e.g., `T extends Number` → `Number`). **Consequences**: (1) `new T()` illegal — compiler doesn't know what T is at runtime. (2) `instanceof List<String>` illegal — at runtime, it's just `List`. (3) Generic exception types illegal — `catch (T e)` impossible. (4) **Bridge methods** generated for covariant overrides — if a subclass narrows a return type, the compiler generates a bridge method with the erased signature that delegates to the specific one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Generics are like LABELS on filing drawers during work hours (compile time): "This drawer is for Cheques ONLY." The label prevents you from putting a withdrawal form in the cheque drawer. But at the END OF THE DAY (runtime), all labels are RIPPED OFF (erasure). Every drawer just says "Object." This means: at runtime, you can't ask "Is this a cheque drawer?" (instanceof List<String>) — all drawers look the same. You can't say "Create a new whatever-is-in-this-drawer" (new T()) — the label is gone.

**One line to remember:** Generics = compile-time labels. Type erasure = labels removed at runtime. At runtime: List<String> = List<Integer> = List. No new T(), no instanceof, bridge methods for covariant overrides.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto generic type erasure and its consequences. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how generic type erasure and its consequences solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a generic repository `Repository<T>` used for Account objects, where the compiler erases the type parameter after checking.

**Step 1.** At compile time the compiler verifies that only Account objects are added for Rajesh and Priya, enforcing full type safety.

**Step 2.** During compilation the type parameter T is erased to its bound (Object), so at runtime the class has no record that it was a repository of Account.

**Step 3.** Because of erasure, operations like `new T()` or `instanceof List<String>` are impossible, and the compiler inserts bridge methods and casts so the stored Account values still come back correctly typed.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ TYPE ERASURE ═══

  COMPILE TIME:                        RUNTIME (after erasure):
  List<String> names                   List names (just List!)
  Box<Integer> box                     Box box (T → Object)
  NumberBox<Double> nb                 NumberBox nb (T → Number)
  Comparable<Account>.compareTo(Account) Comparable.compareTo(Object)

  ═══ WHAT YOU CAN'T DO (because of erasure) ═══
  new T()                    → illegal (T is Object at runtime)
  new T[10]                  → illegal
  instanceof List<String>    → illegal (just List at runtime)
  class MyEx<T> extends Exception → illegal (catch needs concrete type)
  static T field             → illegal (T is instance-level, not class-level)

  ═══ BRIDGE METHODS ═══
  Source:  int compareTo(Account o)
  Erased:  int compareTo(Object o)  ← BRIDGE (generated by compiler)
           { return compareTo((Account) o); }  ← delegates to real method
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
          Compile Time          │        Runtime (JVM)
  ┌──────────────────────────┐  │  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ List<Account> accounts   │  │  │  List  (no type info) │
  │ List<Trade>   trades     │  │  │  List  (same class!)  │
  │  compiler enforces types │──┼─►│  type params ERASED   │
  └──────────────────────────┘  │  └──────────────────────┘
        │ type safety here      │       │ restrictions here
        ▼                       │       ▼
   catches bad add()           │   no new T(), no
   at compile time             │   instanceof List<X>
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     Account implements Comparable<Account>      │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ - balance : BigDecimal                          │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ + compareTo(Account o) : int   ← YOUR method    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │ erasure generates bridge method
        ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Bytecode (after erasure)                      │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  int compareTo(Account) { ...real logic... }    │
  │  int compareTo(Object o) {    ← BRIDGE (synth)  │
  │      return compareTo((Account) o);             │
  │  }                                              │
  │  // T → Object ;  List<Account> → List          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Restrictions: no new T() | no T[] | no catch(T e) │
                no instanceof List<String>           │
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Type erasure means Java generics exist ONLY at compile time — the compiler enforces type safety, then erases all type parameters before generating bytecode. `List<String>` becomes `List`, `T` becomes `Object` (or its bound). At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class. This leads to restrictions: no `new T()` (JVM doesn't know what T is), no `instanceof List<String>` (it's just List), no generic exception types (catch needs concrete classes), and bridge methods generated for covariant overrides.

Bridge methods are synthetic methods the compiler creates to bridge the gap between the erased and specific signatures. When `Account implements Comparable<Account>`, the compiler generates `compareTo(Object)` that casts and delegates to `compareTo(Account)`. Workaround for `new T()`: pass `Class<T>` as a parameter and use reflection (`clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`). In banking: generic repository pattern `Repository<T>` — can't do `new T()` inside the repo, must pass the entity class to the constructor.
